subject: Interpreting distance model output in R

messages.author: d2e6f7c70e669ae3
messages.subject: Interpreting distance model output in R
parts:
Hi all,

This question is asking for help on interpreting summary output of a distance model in R (distance package).  

I am attempting to estimate the abundance of a population of forest birds using distance sampling (point transect).  I have a 20-year data set with many covariates collected with each point.  I have run models with different covariates and done AIC analysis to determine the best model among them.  Here, the model chosen is with a single covariate, Year as a factor.  Also, I should note that in my data, birds are often recorded in groups, or clusters.  So, I set up my model with the necessary tables so that clusters could be accounted for.  Here is the code for my model with hazard rate detection function:

 haam.m8 <- ds(HAAM,key = "hr", transect = "point", truncation = trunc.dist, formula = ~factor(Year), region.table = region.table, sample.table = sample.table, obs.table = obs.table.allspecies, convert.units = 0.001)

I'm having a little difficulty interpreting the R output.  I think I should be able to determine abundance for this species for each year from this output based on the summary of the model.  I hope this is the case, because estimating abundance for each year is one of my objectives for this analysis.

##
 ## Summary for distance analysis
 ## Number of observations :  16535
 ## Distance range         :  0  -  79
 ##
 ## Model : Hazard-rate key function
 ## AIC   : 140233.3
 ##
 ## Detection function parameters
 ## Scale coefficient(s):  
 ##                     estimate         se
 ## (Intercept)       3.48720557 0.04759074
 ## factor(Year)1999 -0.17837882 0.10394015
 ## factor(Year)2000  0.16206740 0.05194754
 ## factor(Year)2001  0.31022523 0.05225895
 ## factor(Year)2002  0.01600722 0.05706552
 ## factor(Year)2003 -0.10458894 0.05449114
 ## factor(Year)2004 -0.03268947 0.05141794
 ## factor(Year)2005  0.05722989 0.05183513
 ## factor(Year)2006  0.15572876 0.05124541
 ## factor(Year)2007  0.41996706 0.05219373
 ## factor(Year)2008  0.54030487 0.05229719
 ## factor(Year)2009  0.27867013 0.05257801
 ## factor(Year)2010  0.32311737 0.05355789
 ## factor(Year)2011  0.33770114 0.05814054
 ## factor(Year)2012  0.32923723 0.05388965
 ## factor(Year)2013  0.39503526 0.05337590
 ## factor(Year)2014  0.38874012 0.05816625
 ## factor(Year)2015  0.26513375 0.05781721
 ## factor(Year)2016  0.23380849 0.05366857
 ## factor(Year)2018  0.30453585 0.08053682
 ##
 ## Shape coefficient(s):  
 ##             estimate         se
 ## (Intercept) 1.309443 0.01848787
 ##
 ##                         Estimate           SE         CV
 ## Average p           4.033117e-01 4.566239e-03 0.01132186
 ## N in covered region 4.099807e+04 5.286408e+02 0.01289429


Do I need to back-transform the coefficients, and then put them into an equation including observations for that year in order to get year-specific abundances?  Also, do I need to incorporate the shape coefficients at all?

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Interpreting distance model output in R
parts:
Brian

Quite a large data set you have there.  I recognise this is not the question you asked, but with 16000 observations spread across 20 years, seems you ought to have sufficient data within each year to analyse years separately.  You can see that the CV on your estimate of detection probability is 1%, so even if some precision is lost as a result of fitting models with more parameters (2 parameters per year for the HR), the precision cost is unlikely to be too high.

A couple of other observations regarding your output.  The yearly coefficients are positive for all years but 3; meaning that detection probability is higher than in the first year of the study (1998) for all years but those 3.  Was 1998 an abnormally poor year for detecting birds?  I also note that the average detection probability across all years is 0.04; does that seem plausible?  Is this dataset filtered for Hawaiian amakihi as your object name suggests?

What you have reproduced is the summary of the "ddf" portion of the ds object.  Abundance and density estimates are in the "dht" portion of the ds object.  Scratching my head about this for a bit, you might be able to produce your year-specific abundance estimates by feeding the "haam.m8" object into the dht2() function in Distance (new to the Distance package in version 0.9.9 downloaded via remotes::install_github("distancedevelopment/Distance")

yearly.abund <- dht2(haam.m8, strat_formula=~Year, stratification="geographical")

Yes, I realise your strata are not geographical, but I think this might be the way to specify the year-specific abundance estimates.  See how that works, we may need to correspond off-list to get it just right.

Hi Eric,

Thanks for your reply.  Yes, the species here is Hawaii amakihi and out of 10 other species I am analyzing, it has the most observations by far. 

It is possible that year 1998 was a poor detection year in comparison to subsequent years, perhaps because it was our first year and we were still developing/perfecting survey field methods.  Isn't the average detectability across all years 0.4 and not 0.04?  0.4 seems plausible to me, 0.04 does not. 

I take your point about the large data set and that I probably could analyze the years separately; however, this data set needs to be broken apart into 3 subsets based on geographical area, as there were 3 distinct general regions where data were collected.  I need to do this for other species, and most other species have significantly less observations than the HAAM dataset.  Given that I will not have the luxury of large datasets for all species, I'd like to determine the most efficient modeling process possible.   

I successfully installed the DistanceDevelopment/Distance package and attempted to run the dht2 function and got the error:

Error in dht2(haam.m8, strat_formula = ~Year, stratification = "geographical") : 
  Need to supply either observations, transects and geo_strat OR flatfile

I'm not sure if the dht2() function is designed for distance datasets where the observations are clusters of birds, and not binary (my dataset is formatted for clusters)?

I know that when clusters do not have to be accounted for, one can give the ds() function a flatfile with "region.label" as a variable, and the output breaks abundance estimates apart by geographical region.  As pointed out earlier, I do not have 1 flatfile, but several tables that I feed to the model because I have to account for clustered individuals.  Here is what those tables look like:

parts:
Brian

There are more layers to the onion than there first appeared with multiple species and geographic strata entering the picture.  Let's work through the elements.

First, apologies for two errors on my part:

  • You are correct that average detectability is 0.4 not 0.04, my mistake.
  • Second error of mine was to not provide complete syntax for the call to dht2.  The error message returned from dht2 was asking that you provide your obs.table, sample.table and region.table data frames for arguments "observation", "transect" and "geo_strat" respectively; with "year" being treated as a stratification covariate.  With the news that there exists genuine geographic stratification in the survey design, this approach is no longer valid unless you intend to conduct three separate analyses, one for each geographic stratum.  If you are happy to conduct separate analyses for each stratum, then consider the flatfile approach described below.

With regard to birds occurring in groups, your data can be organised in the "flatfile" format, including an additional field that must be named "size" for group size.  There is no necessity that the region.table, sample.table and obs.table style of data input be used (despite the impression given by the documentation for the ds() function).  Adopting the flatfile data format ought to smooth your analysis of multiple datasets.

From what I gather, the analysis you wish to conduct would produce year- and stratum-specific estimates of density taking into account group size for HAAM (and nine other species).

I believe the "proper" way to do this would be to use two-level stratification.  Theoretically, dht2 was designed to accept syntax such as this:

strat_formula=~Year+Region.Label

however this is untested.  What you want is on the edge of what the Distance package is currently able to do.  If you are under time pressure to complete the analyses, you might need to take a more 'production line' approach filtering data by year and strata, fitting detection functions and producing abundance estimates.  For data-poor species, you might need a more elegant approach treating either year or strata as covariates, bringing you back to your original question, where you may be able to employ dht2.  Feel free to correspond further off list.
